source_text: Quid ergo tibi opitulari potest, quod ego inter commixtionem sexuum, fecunditatem coeuntium, nolui concupiscentiae nomine lacerare, cum eam nec tu cum Manichaeo diabolicam potueris approbare; et iam ipsa praemissae disputationis consequentia claruisset, ad eiusdem operam recurrere sensum illam, quo commixtorum corpus afficitur, ad cuius institutionem corpora, coniugia semina referrentur?
pass_a_gloss: What therefore can help you, that I was unwilling, among the mingling of the sexes, the fertility of those coupling, to tear by the name of desire, when neither have you with Manichaeus been able to prove it diabolical; and already by the very consequence of the preceding disputation it had become clear that that sense recurs to its work, by which the body of those mingled is affected, to whose institution bodies, marriages, seeds were referred?

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: What help, then, can you gain from my unwillingness, amid discussion of the union of the sexes and the fertility of those who join together, to disparage it by the name of desire? Neither you nor Manichaeus has been able to prove that it is devilish. And the very sequence of the preceding argument had already made it clear that this sensation, which affects the bodies of those who unite, goes back to the work of the same one whose institution accounts for bodies, marriages, and seeds.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
